COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

============================================================  

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Chosen method: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental‐variables design that exploits the interaction of (i) compulsory‐school‐leaving-age (CSLA) laws that bind until a fixed birthday in the calendar year and (ii) the individual’s quarter of birth.  

Rationale  
• In almost every U.S. state, children can start 1st grade in September of the calendar year in which they turn six. A child born in Q1 (Jan–Mar) therefore starts school almost a year older than a child born in Q4 (Oct–Dec).  
• CSLA laws historically required students to stay in school until their 16th (sometimes 17th) birthday. Conditional on grade started, Q1 births therefore hit the legal drop-out age roughly one grade earlier than Q4 births.  
• Because quarter of birth is predetermined and plausibly orthogonal to unobserved ability, it serves as a quasi-random shock to completed schooling. The 2SLS estimate recovers the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for “compliers”—students whose schooling decisions are altered by the interaction of CSLA and birth quarter.  

Why not RDD alone?  
Running an RD in date of birth is possible but less transparent because the assignment variable is circular (Jan 1 = 0 degrees ≈ Dec 31). Treating quarter dummies as instruments in a 2SLS framework is cleaner and widely replicable across data sets and decades.  

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
• S (continuous): completed years of schooling.  

Instrument (first-stage “treatment”)  
• Z = set of three binary indicators for being born in Q1, Q2, or Q3 (Q4 omitted).  

Control group / counterfactual  
• Individuals born in Q4 serve as the baseline.  

Treatment timing  
• The “event” occurs at the 16th (or 17th) birthday, when the legal option to drop out first differs by quarter-of-birth. Because all observations are taken in adulthood, treatment timing is implicit in the construction of the instrument.  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
------------------------------------------------------------  
IV-A1 (Relevance): Quarter of birth must be correlated with years of schooling.  
• Highly plausible; well-documented first-stage F-statistics above 15–20 in CPS and Census data.  

IV-A2 (Exclusion): Quarter of birth affects adult earnings only through its effect on schooling, not through any other channel.  
• Plausible in U.S. setting: season of birth is uncorrelated with ability, parent SES, or local labor demand once we control for state, cohort, gender, and race fixed effects. Remaining worries (health endowments, school cohort effects) are addressed in Section 4.  

IV-A3 (Independence): Conditional on controls, quarter of birth is as-good-as-random with respect to unobserved determinants of earnings.  
• Supported by balance tests on parental education, race, and sibling outcomes.  

IV-A4 (Monotonicity): No “defiers”—nobody born in an early quarter because they want to obtain *more* schooling by dropping out later.  
• Institutionally plausible: parents do not time births for such fine educational reasons.  

IV-A5 (SUTVA): One person’s quarter of birth does not affect another’s earnings (no spillovers).  
• Reasonable given the large labor market and small treatment share.  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Season-of-birth effects on health endowments (e.g., prenatal nutrition, disease exposure) could violate exclusion.  
Mitigation:  
• Control flexibly for state-of-birth × month-of-birth climate variables.  
• Replicate analyses on subsamples where health channels are minimal (white non-farm males) and show similar 2SLS estimates.  

Threat 2: Variation in school-starting-age policies across states and over time may weaken or confound the first stage.  
Mitigation:  
• Include state-of-birth × cohort fixed effects so identification is purely within state-cohort.  
• Report first-stage F-statistics by decade and drop states/periods with idiosyncratic rules.  

Threat 3: Labor market quarter-of-birth discrimination (e.g., older workers in a cohort may earn more).  
Mitigation:  
• Include potential experience, age, and age-squared controls; the exclusion restriction only requires that any direct age effect be additive and separable from schooling.  
• Placebo test: run the same 2SLS on outcomes that schooling should not affect (e.g., height, number of siblings).  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  
------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Required packages
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # 2SLS and clustering
library(modelsummary) # nice tables
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov

# 1. Load CPS March pooled 1994–1996 (pre-cleaned to one CSV)
cps <- fread("cps_94_96.csv")

# 2. Variable construction
cps[, qob := fifelse(monthborn %in% 1:3, 1,
              fifelse(monthborn %in% 4:6, 2,
              fifelse(monthborn %in% 7:9, 3, 4)))]
cps[, q1 := as.integer(qob == 1)]
cps[, q2 := as.integer(qob == 2)]
cps[, q3 := as.integer(qob == 3)]      # Q4 is omitted
cps[, yrs_school := educ]              # assume educ already in years
cps[, ln_earn := log(annual_earnings)] # trim below min wage, top-code
cps[, age2 := age^2]

# 3. Main 2SLS: ln earnings on schooling IVed by QOB
iv_formula <- ln_earn ~ yrs_school + age + age2 + race + sex + factor(state) + factor(cohort) | 
                         age + age2 + race + sex + factor(state) + factor(cohort) + q1 + q2 + q3

iv_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = cps, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state_cohort)

etable(iv_main, se = "cluster")

# 4. Robustness check 1: Include month-of-birth dummies to soak up health seasonality
cps[, mob := factor(monthborn)]
iv_rb1 <- feols(update(iv_formula, . ~ . + mob | . | . ~ . + mob), 
                data = cps, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state_cohort)

# 5. Robustness check 2: Run reduced-form for log earnings on QOB directly
rf <- feols(ln_earn ~ q1 + q2 + q3 + age + age2 + race + sex + factor(state) + factor(cohort),
            data = cps, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state_cohort)

# 6. Print summary
modelsummary(list(Main = iv_main, "+MoB" = iv_rb1, "Reduced-Form" = rf),
             statistic = "std.error", estimate = "estimate")
```  

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (human-capital) predicts a positive causal return to schooling. Previous U.S. estimates using similar designs cluster around 7–10 percent higher annual earnings per additional year of education. My prior: 2SLS coefficient ≈ 0.08 (≈ 8 %) with a standard error of ≈ 0.015.  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT  
------------------------------------------------------------  
(C1–C5 use the IV-specific checklist)  

C1 Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10): 1  
C2 Exclusion restriction (no direct effect on Y): 0.7  
C3 Independence / as-good-as-random: 0.8  
C4 Monotonicity / no defiers: 0.9  
C5 SUTVA / no interference: 1  

Average score ≈ 0.88 → Overall, the design is strong but still vulnerable to small violations of exclusion through health seasonality.
